newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Highlights of U.N. reform plans.
newsitem.headline: Highlights of U.N. reform plans.

text.p: Following are highlights of Secretary-General Kofi Annan's 90-page reform plans for the United Nations. Some plans need to be approved by U.N. government bodies, such as the General Assembly.

-- DEVELOPMENT FUND - Savings achieved by the elimination of 1,000 jobs announced previously, cuts in administrative structures would go to a new fund for the economic development of poor countries. The money is estimated at about $200 million by the year 2002.

-- DEPUTY - Create a deputy secretary-general post, preferably a woman, to take charge of issues that need more collaboration among its many separate organs. The General Assembly has to approve this job.

-- CABINET - Establish a cabinet-style structure that would prevent 27 senior officials reporting directly to Annan. Instead four managers would take charge of specific areas for peace and security, humanitarian affairs, development and economic and social issues. Another four or five managers, including a human rights official, will join the group. Twelve entities in the main bureaucracy would be merged into five.

-- AID AGENCIES - Six agencies are to be coordinated in two main groups -- humanitarian affairs and development. But each agency would maintain its identity. The aim is closer coordination to make sure common facilities are developed in each country where more than one agency operates. Together the six, dealing with refugees, children, development and food have thousands more employees than the 9,000 in the main bureaucracy that reports directly to Annan.
-- CRIME - Consolidate scattered UN programmes for drugs, crime, money laundering, terrorism, drug trafficking, under a single administration in Vienna.
-- HUMAN RIGHTS - High Commissioner for human rights would be in charge of the Centre for Human Rights in Geneva also.

-- DISARMAMENT - Create a new disarmament department integrating existing programmes and centres in New York to prevent the proliferation of all types of weapons and control or monitor flow of arms to conflict areas.

-- BUDGET - Proposals to stop the General Assembly from micromanaging programmes in deciding on level of each post and other details. Instead Annan wants to be judged on results within the objectives and funding limits and let his managers decide the best way to get the job done.

-- GENERAL ASSEMBLY -- Recommends the 185-nation body streamline it agenda of 165 items and set priorities for its various programmes. Member states should also reduce five intergovernmental bodies into two.
-- SUNSET CLAUSE - Recommends an expiry date for any new programmes established, making sure the project would end unless specifically renewed.

-- ALL AGENCIES - Recommends a commission made up of government ministers for the year 2,000 to look at the byzantine system of specialised agencies, ranging from semi-autonomous groups to those completely independent of the secretary-general, such as the World Bank.

-- REVOLVING FUND - Help solve the cash flow problem by asking for contributions from member countries for those nations, like the United States, who are heavily in arrears. Interest would have to be paid by the borrowers to the lenders. The idea is bound to be rejected.
